relations.note: Reconstructed as Ninazu’s early emblem within his ophidian and chthonic circle.
Horned serpent-dragons attend him and emerge from his shoulders.
Tišpak rides or stands upon the serpent-dragon as his controlled animal.
Tišpak kills the giant lion-serpent and wins kingship; identification as mušḫuššu is disputed.

relations.myth: Birth of the destructive Labbu dragon
relations.note: Enlil designs or authorizes the monster’s birth in the fragmentary Labbu tradition.

relations.myth: Birth of the destructive Labbu dragon
relations.note: Sea brings forth the monster; its personification and identification with Tiamat remain disputed.

relations.myth: Birth of the destructive Labbu dragon
relations.note: River joins Sea in bringing forth the destructive monster.

relations.myth: Tiamat creates eleven monsters for war
relations.note: Tiamat creates or musters the mušḫuššu among her eleven monstrous troops.
Marduk defeats and binds Tiamat’s host, including the mušḫuššu.
The conquered dragon becomes Marduk’s mount, emblem, guardian, and bearer of his spade.
The dragon supports Nabû’s stylus, sometimes alongside Marduk’s spade.
Sennacherib-era theology places Aššur upon Marduk’s serpent-dragon.

relations.myth: Monumental setting at the Ishtar Gate
relations.note: Marduk’s dragons decorate Ištar’s named gate, but are not her animals.

relations.myth: Bulls and dragons alternate at Ishtar Gate
relations.note: Adad’s bulls alternate monumentally with Marduk’s mušḫuššu-dragons.

relations.myth: Divine symbols share seals and kudurrus
relations.note: Sîn’s symbol appears beside the dragon-bearing emblem of Marduk.
Šamaš’s symbol shares legal-symbolic registers with the mušḫuššu.
Anu’s symbol shares legal-symbolic registers with the mušḫuššu.
Enlil’s symbol shares legal-symbolic registers with the mušḫuššu.
Ea’s symbol shares legal-symbolic registers with the mušḫuššu without narrative interaction.
